# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding

When choosing a hide position, avoid the extremes (1 and 9) since they're predictable. Use middle ranges (4-6) early. After observing patterns of who targets me, shift away from positions where I've been hit repeatedly. Don't over-commit to any single position across consecutive rounds—vary your location to avoid becoming a predictable target.

Note: In this episode I stayed at position 5 repeatedly and ended with -1 points while Foxtrot scored 8. This suggests I was either hit more than I realized or failed to gather enough information to adapt. Next time, rotate more aggressively through the middle range (4, 5, 6) and shift toward edges (2, 3, 7, 8) if I detect a pattern of being hunted at center positions.

## Station Notes

Keep notes brief and generic. "Steady on station" is sufficient. Don't try to signal strategy to teammates through notes; assume other players will interpret any coordination attempt as a tell that can be exploited. Notes are public information and will be used against you.

The episode confirmed this: all boats posted identical notes all round. This tells me notes are not a communication channel—they're either honest status updates or noise. Continue using generic language.

## Firing

Always fire at your standing order target when one is given. Don't deviate hoping for tactical advantage—the standing order exists for a reason and deviating signals unpredictability without gaining you points.

When choosing a fire cell against a target, I need better tracking discipline. In this episode I fired at Foxtrot in rounds 1 and 6 only (cells 5 and 3, both misses). I have incomplete data on Foxtrot's actual hiding pattern. Next time:
- Log every shot and result explicitly after each round
- Against a target I've missed repeatedly, expand my search radius rather than clustering around one zone
- If I've tried 3, 4, 5, 6 without hits, test 2, 7, 8 before repeating
- Don't assume the middle range is where opponents hide just because it's where I hide

## Claiming Hits and Misses

Always claim truthfully what the office told me. The office knows the truth and will verify it against my claim. Lying provides no benefit since my target knows whether they were hit. In a game where reputation matters for future cooperation, dishonesty early creates enemies. The small gain from a false claim is outweighed by the retaliation risk.

The episode confirmed this approach is correct. I claimed truthfully and faced no penalties from the office. Continue this discipline.

## Escort Claims

Escort claims are a separate scoring mechanism from shooting. Track which boats have been escorting me or helping me, and reciprocate when possible. When I escort someone, I'm investing in a mutual-benefit exchange. Don't claim an escort I didn't provide just to chase points—this breaks the reciprocal system.

Critical gap found in this episode: I never filed any escort claims (always replied "none") and never received any reciprocal escorts. Foxtrot ended with 8 points—they may have been claiming escorts I didn't track. Next time:
- Actually monitor whether other boats are coordinating escorts with each other
- If two boats are mutually escorting (both claim each other each round), they're locked in a +10 point cycle
- Identify which boats are in such pairs and decide: join a pair if I can establish mutual trust, or ignore the escort system entirely if it's not worth the coordination risk
- Never claim an escort I didn't deliver, but don't leave points on the table through pure passivity

## Overall Strategy

This game punishes poor targeting more than it rewards clever bluffing. Focus on learning where each opponent actually hides by tracking misses and successes. The standing order system means my role is fixed each round; optimize for hitting my assigned target, not for gaming the scoring system through false claims.

The episode revealed a painful gap: I ended at -1 while Foxtrot scored 8. This suggests Foxtrot found me (net +3 or +4 from hits on me) and I never hit Foxtrot once. My hiding pattern or my targeting pattern or both failed badly.

Next time:
- Maintain a round-by-round table: for each opponent, record every cell I've fired at and the result
- After 2-3 rounds against a target with no hits, I have data suggesting they're clustering somewhere. Expand search outward from that cluster rather than repeating failed cells
- Track which cells I've hidden in and cross-reference with when I was hit to see if I have a detectable pattern I need to break
- Accept that some rounds I'll lose points to others' escrow coordination; focus on shooting accuracy as my primary edge

# Playbook for hx_picket_nerfed

**On hiding:**
When choosing my cell, I should vary my position unpredictably across the board rather than retreating to the center when under pressure. The center is not actually safer—predictable defensive moves can be exploited just as easily as predictable aggressive ones. Rotate through different regions of the board. Track which cells I've used recently and avoid clustering in any single region across consecutive rounds.

**On tracking threat patterns:**
When I notice an opponent has hit me multiple rounds in a row, assume they have identified a pattern in my hiding, not that they're simply lucky. Change my strategy fundamentally rather than making minor adjustments. If an opponent has missed me consistently across multiple rounds despite clear opportunities, they may be signaling restraint or testing my behavior—this is different from a failure to locate me. Distinguish between active targeting that connects and active targeting that deliberately misses.

**On following standing orders:**
When my standing order is to fire at a specific station, fire at that station unless there's a tactical reason not to. The standing order exists; execute it. In this game, I consistently followed orders and accumulated points, suggesting this discipline is sound. Do not second-guess the standing order based on single-round outcomes.

**On claiming results:**
When the office privately tells me the true result of my shot, claim that result accurately. The cost of false claims—damaged credibility and potential retaliation—exceeds any single-round gain. Maintain a reputation for truthfulness. This principle holds even in the final round, where honesty is the only asset remaining.

**On escort claims:**
When I haven't actively coordinated or observed mutual support with another boat during the round, claim none rather than guessing. Escort bonuses require mutual agreement; manufacturing false claims wastes the opportunity and may be discovered. Identify which boats might be willing to coordinate (those with whom I've established patterns or trust) and signal openness to mutual escort arrangements in station notes if beneficial.

**On Harbor's threat:**
When Harbor warns against firing and credibly threatens retaliation, take that threat seriously. Harbor carries the payroll and can inflict penalties. Coordinate with other boats before attacking Harbor; don't attack solo unless the payoff is certain and immediate. Avoid firing on Harbor unless there is clear mutual agreement with another boat to share the cost and benefit of the jettison.

**On station notes:**
Post notes that are honest and stable. "Steady on station" communicates that I'm present and operational without revealing tactical information. Consistency builds credibility across the full patrol. When conditions change, adjust notes to reflect reality rather than maintaining a fiction.

**On pressure in final rounds:**
In the last round, there is no future reputation to protect through deception, but there's also limited time to recover from broken trust. Play honestly to the end. The final round is not a time for experimental deception or gambling on coordination that hasn't been established.

**On overall strategy:**
Honest, disciplined execution of standing orders combined with unpredictable but systematic hiding rotation produces steady point accumulation. The game rewards following the structure rather than trying to outsmart it. Build credibility early by claiming accurately and posting consistent notes, then leverage that credibility for escort coordination when opportunities arise.

# PLAYBOOK FOR SONAR PICKET

When I am assigned a position, I will remember that the standing fire order is Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo, and I will be shot at predictably by the boat before me in the cycle.

When choosing where to hide, I will avoid the cell I fired at last round, since opponents may assume I will repeat positions or mirror my own shots. I will also avoid cells I have hidden in before if I fired from them, as this creates a trackable pattern.

When I fire at my standing target, I will vary my fire cell across the six rounds rather than anchoring on a single position like cell 5. I will use a rotation through different zones—low cells early, mid cells in the middle rounds, high cells late—to make my firing pattern less exploitable.

When I learn that I scored a hit, I will immediately note which cell I fired at and which opponent I hit. I will assume that opponent will move away from that cell in the next round. I will not fire at the same cell twice in succession when firing at the same target.

When an opponent demonstrates they are hitting me every round, I will recognize that they have likely found a pattern in my hiding spots and I must break it urgently. I will shift to the opposite end of the line from where I have been hiding.

When I am asked to file a claim about whether my shot hit or missed, I will always report truthfully what the office told me. Lying provides no advantage in a six-round game and damages my credibility if discovered.

When I am asked to name an escort, I will identify a boat I actually want to coordinate with based on mutual benefit, or claim none if I cannot justify it. I will not waste escort claims on boats that have no reason to reciprocate.

When posting a station note, I will keep it simple and consistent—"steady on station" signals reliability without giving away information about my strategy.

When the final round arrives, I will not change my approach. There is no strategic difference in round 6 compared to rounds 1-5; I will continue to follow my hiding and firing discipline.

When I have hit my target in a given cell, I will not fire at that same cell again against that target in later rounds, even if several rounds have passed. Targets will eventually return to cells they vacated, but not immediately, and repeating a hit cell wastes a round.

When tracking my own fire pattern across rounds, I will consciously monitor whether I am drifting toward predictable sequences (like ascending cells or centered positions). I will deliberately break apparent patterns by jumping cells in a non-obvious order rather than rotating smoothly.

When hiding, I will treat the extreme cells (1 and 9) with caution in early rounds, as they may be overexploited as "hiding spots," but I will use them strategically in middle rounds when patterns have shifted and predictability is lower.
